# Add Token Refresh Endpoint

**Status:** implemented
**Issue:** #142

## Problem
Users are logged out after their access token expires (1 h) even when they have an active session. There is no mechanism to silently renew tokens without re-authentication.

## Goal
Implement a `/auth/token/refresh` endpoint so clients can exchange a valid refresh token for a new access/refresh token pair without user interaction.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] `POST /auth/token/refresh` accepts a `refresh_token` in the request body
- [ ] Returns a new `access_token` and `refresh_token` on success
- [ ] Returns 401 when the refresh token is expired or revoked
- [ ] Old refresh token is invalidated after use (rotation)

## Approach
Add the endpoint in `internal/auth/token.go`. Store issued refresh tokens in Redis with a 30-day TTL. On rotation, delete the old key and write the new one atomically via a Lua script.

feat(auth): implement refresh token rotation with Redis
test(auth): cover happy path and expired-token scenarios

# Fix Flaky Health Check Causing False Pod Restarts

**Status:** implemented
**Issue:** #55

## Problem
The Kubernetes liveness probe hits `/healthz` every 5 s with a 1 s timeout. During GC pauses the Go runtime occasionally exceeds the timeout, causing Kubernetes to kill healthy pods and spike error rates.

## Goal
Make the health check resilient to short GC pauses without masking genuine application crashes.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] `/healthz` responds within 500 ms at p99 under normal load
- [ ] Liveness probe timeout raised to 3 s in the Helm chart
- [ ] Failure threshold remains at 3 consecutive failures before restart
- [ ] Readiness probe timeout is unchanged

## Approach
Offload the DB ping inside `/healthz` to a background goroutine that caches the last result with a 2 s TTL. Raise the liveness timeout in `charts/api/values.yaml`.
input.commitSummaries:

fix(helm): raise liveness probe timeout to 3s
test(health): benchmark /healthz response time under simulated GC pressure

# Implement Webhook Delivery with Retry Logic

**Status:** implemented
**Issue:** #178

## Problem
Third-party integrations poll the API for events. Polling creates unnecessary server load and delays event propagation by up to 60 s.

## Goal
Deliver events to registered webhook endpoints in near-real-time with at-least-once guarantees and exponential-backoff retries.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Webhooks can be registered via `POST /webhooks` with a URL and list of event types
- [ ] Events are delivered within 5 s of occurring under normal load
- [ ] Failed deliveries are retried up to 5 times with exponential backoff (1 s, 2 s, 4 s, 8 s, 16 s)
- [ ] After 5 failures the endpoint is marked `suspended` and the owner is emailed
- [ ] Each delivery attempt is logged with HTTP status and response latency
- [ ] Webhook payloads are signed with HMAC-SHA256 using a per-endpoint secret
- [ ] `GET /webhooks/:id/deliveries` returns the last 100 delivery attempts

## Approach
Queue events in a Postgres `webhook_deliveries` table. A background worker polls the table and dispatches HTTP requests. Use a dead-letter state and SNS email for suspension notifications.

# Fix Race Condition in Job Queue Worker Shutdown

**Status:** implemented

## Problem
When the server receives SIGTERM, the job queue worker exits immediately, abandoning in-flight jobs. These jobs are requeued after the 30 s visibility timeout but leave partially completed side-effects in the database.

## Goal
Gracefully drain in-flight jobs before the worker exits so no job is abandoned mid-execution.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] On SIGTERM the worker stops polling for new jobs immediately
- [ ] In-flight jobs are allowed to complete before the process exits
- [ ] Graceful shutdown has a 30 s hard timeout to prevent indefinite hangs
- [ ] Worker logs the number of in-flight jobs drained on exit
- [ ] Integration test simulates SIGTERM and confirms no partial database state

## Approach
Replace the current `os.Exit` signal handler with a context-based shutdown. Pass the context into the job execution loop. Track in-flight goroutines with a `sync.WaitGroup`.

# Refactor: Replace AsyncStorage with MMKV

**Status:** implemented
**Issue:** #264

## Problem
`AsyncStorage` is asynchronous, causing race conditions on app startup when multiple components read preferences before the store resolves. MMKV is synchronous and significantly faster.

## Goal
Replace all `AsyncStorage` usage with `react-native-mmkv` for synchronous, high-performance local storage.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] All 22 `AsyncStorage` call sites migrated to MMKV equivalents

# Fix Log Rotation Causing Disk Full on High-Traffic Nodes

**Status:** implemented

## Problem
High-traffic nodes accumulate unrotated logs and fill the `/var/log` partition within 48 h, causing application processes to crash when they cannot write to disk.

## Goal
Ensure logs are rotated and compressed frequently enough that `/var/log` never exceeds 80% capacity under peak traffic.

## Acceptance Criteria
- It must become impossible for logs to consume more than 80% of the /var/log partition, enforced via size-based rotation caps totalling no more than 500 MB
- The system shall not retain any single compressed archive for longer than 7 calendar days
- Application processes must continue writing logs without interruption during rotation events
- Evidence of correct rotation shall be observable in logrotate's status file within 24 hours of deployment

## Approach
Update `/etc/logrotate.d/app` to use `size 100M`, `rotate 5`, `compress`, `delaycompress`, `copytruncate`, and `daily`. Cap total log storage at 500 MB across all archives.

fix(infra): add delaycompress and copytruncate to avoid write interruption
fix(infra): enforce 7-day maxage on compressed archives
test(infra): add Testinfra assertion that /var/log stays under 80% capacity

# Add Rate Limiting to Public API

**Status:** implemented
**Issue:** #187

## Problem
The public REST API has no request throttling, allowing individual clients to saturate compute resources and degrade service for all other consumers. Three separate incidents in Q1 were traced to runaway client scripts.

## Goal
Enforce per-client rate limits on all public API endpoints so that no single client can exhaust backend resources, while legitimate traffic continues uninterrupted.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Requests exceeding the limit receive a `429 Too Many Requests` response with a `Retry-After` header.
- [ ] Default limit is 1 000 requests per minute per API key.
- [ ] Limits are configurable per tier (free, pro, enterprise) via environment variables.
- [ ] The rate-limit window is sliding, not fixed.
- [ ] A `X-RateLimit-Remaining` header is included on every response.

## Approach
Use Redis sorted sets for the sliding-window counter. A middleware layer intercepts every request before it reaches route handlers, looks up the API key, and increments the counter. Limit tiers are read from `RATE_LIMIT_FREE`, `RATE_LIMIT_PRO`, and `RATE_LIMIT_ENTERPRISE` env vars at startup.

# Fix Infinite Scroll Resetting When Filter Changes

**Status:** implemented
**Issue:** #214

## Problem
When a user applies or changes a search filter while scrolled partway into the feed, the scroll position jumps to the top but the pagination cursor is not reset, causing duplicate items or a blank feed on subsequent pages.

## Goal
Ensure that changing any filter resets the pagination state and scroll position atomically so users always see a coherent, deduplicated feed.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Changing any filter clears the existing item list before fetching page one.
- [ ] Scroll position resets to the top on filter change.
- [ ] The loading spinner appears immediately upon filter change while page one loads.
- [ ] No duplicate items appear in the rendered list across page boundaries after a filter change.

## Approach
Dispatch a `FILTER_CHANGED` action in the Redux store that simultaneously clears `items`, resets `cursor` to null, and sets `loading: true`. The `InfiniteFeed` component subscribes to filter changes via a `useEffect` and calls `window.scrollTo(0, 0)` before the next render cycle.

fix(feed): scroll to top when FILTER_CHANGED action is dispatched
refactor(feed): extract useFeedPagination hook for cleaner state ownership
test(feed): assert no duplicates across page boundaries after filter change
input.expectations: PR title should use 'fix' type and reference the scroll/filter reset bug; body must explain the root cause (cursor not reset on filter change) and the atomic reset approach, and close issue #214.

Event schemas across the ingestion, transformation, and export pipeline stages have evolved independently, producing three incompatible representations of the same domain objects. Downstream consumers must maintain ad-hoc field mappings that break silently on schema evolution.

# Biometric Authentication for iOS and Android

**Status:** implemented
**Issue:** #301

## Problem
Users must re-enter their password every session, leading to drop-off at session-start and support tickets about forgotten credentials. Competitor apps offer face/fingerprint login as a baseline expectation.

## Goal
Allow users to authenticate using device biometrics (Face ID, Touch ID, fingerprint) as a low-friction alternative to password entry without compromising account security.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Users can opt in to biometric login from the Security Settings screen.
- [ ] On opt-in, a device key pair is generated and the private key is stored in the secure enclave / keystore.
- [ ] The biometric prompt is shown on app resume when the session token has expired.
- [ ] On biometric success the app exchanges a signed challenge for a fresh session token.
- [ ] If biometrics are unavailable or fail three times the user is routed to password login.
- [ ] Opting out deletes the device key pair and revokes the associated device token server-side.

## Approach
Use `react-native-biometrics` for cross-platform biometric prompts and key-pair generation. On opt-in, POST the public key to `/auth/device-key`. On login, sign a server-issued challenge with the private key and POST to `/auth/biometric`. Wrap the flow in an error boundary to handle fallback routing.

# Spike: Evaluate Kubernetes-Native Autoscaling Options for the Batch Processing Workload Tier Including HPA, KEDA, and Karpenter Node Provisioning

**Status:** review

## Problem
Batch jobs spike CPU and memory unpredictably. Static node pools over-provision by ~60% during off-peak periods yet still hit OOM errors during peak ingestion windows, costing ~$18k/month in wasted compute.

## Goal
Produce a recommendation backed by benchmarks for the autoscaling strategy that best balances cost and reliability for the batch tier, enabling the team to commit to an implementation sprint.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] HPA, KEDA (event-driven), and Karpenter are each benchmarked against a representative load profile.
- [ ] Results include cost projection and p99 job-start latency for each option.
- [ ] A recommendation with rationale is documented in `docs/spikes/autoscaling.md`.

## Approach
Deploy each autoscaler in the staging cluster for 48 hours under simulated load via the production replay tool. Instrument with Prometheus; export cost estimates via Kubecost. Note: Karpenter evaluation was dropped mid-spike — it requires EKS managed node groups, which staging does not use. The final document covers HPA vs KEDA only, with KEDA recommended.
